commonPoints: A tripod steadies binoculars so you see more detail than hand-held
Binoculars need a tripod adapter that threads into the center hinge
Stability and weight trade against each other; carbon saves weight
Pan or fluid heads beat ball heads for scanning
Height matters most for standing use and for looking up at the sky

ourGain.point: Height ladder from maker specs: Summit Carbon II 53.3 in, SLIK CF-733 52 in column down / 65.5 in up, SIRUI ST-124 62.2 in, BOG 59 in, Ridgeview 73.8 in; the 20.5 in gap between Summit and Ridgeview decides seated vs standing glassing.

Load headroom against a 75 oz (about 4.7 lb) Celestron SkyMaster 20x80: the SIRUI VA-5 kit's 6.6 lb rating leaves under 2 lb spare, while the Vortex kits (22 lb) and SLIK legs (33.1 lb) leave plenty; the head, not the legs, sets the limit.
Chooser by situation: backcountry seated glassing, standing glassing, budget smooth fluid head, buy-the-legs-and-head-separately, glass and shoot from one clamp.
ourGain.source: our decision rule from the specs above

ourGain.point: Sticky pan heads that jump while scanning: owners fix it with a fluid head (SIRUI VA-5) or a damped 2-way head rather than new legs.

painPoints.pain: A ball head lets the spotting scope or big binocular flop over when unlocked
painPoints.details: Ball heads release every axis at once; glassers prefer pan or fluid heads with separate pan and tilt.

quotes.text: Ball heads work to only they are sensitive when you unlock the optic as they can move wherever.

painPoints.pain: A light backpacking tripod wobbles at full height with heavy glass
painPoints.details: Owners report light carbon legs spreading or wiggling at full extension with big optics, but solid when sitting.

quotes.text: Using an 85mm scope on light duty tripods, with legs fully extended, is an unrealistic expectation and muddies the water.

painPoints.pain: With binoculars on a tripod you have to stoop to look up at the sky
painPoints.details: When binoculars point upward the eyepieces drop below the tripod's top, so even a 69 in tripod leaves many observers bending; a taller tripod shakes more, and sitting puts the chair in the legs.

quotes.text: It will likely require you to stoop when viewing.

painPoints.details: Beginners with 25x70 or 20x80 binoculars find a light camera tripod shakes; replies point to heavier legs and fluid heads.

quotes.text: I tried a standard camera tripod. Too shaky.
